Maladaptive Strategies.value: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
try hard not think about the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette:
For fifty years, Dr. An Nguyen's hands had been his life. As a surgeon, they represented precision, control, and an unwavering calm that had saved countless lives. Now, at seventy-seven and semi-retired, he regarded them as alien things, prone to trembling for reasons he couldn't command. The breakdown had begun six months earlier, during what should have been a routine appendectomy he was supervising. A faulty electrocautery unit sparked, igniting the surgical drapes in a flash of shocking heat and acrid smoke. He remembered the smell most vividly-a foul mix of burning plastic and something horribly organic-and the sight of the young resident closest to the machine, her scrubs alight. An was pulled back by a nurse before he could react, a helpless witness to the chaos and the smell of burning that filled the operating room.

In the weeks that followed, An tried to impose his surgeon's discipline on his own mind. He refused to discuss the incident, attempting to wall it off through sheer force of will. He found himself trying hard not to think about the trauma, a constant, exhausting effort of suppression. This strategy, however, only seemed to make the memory more volatile and strange. When fragments of the event surfaced, they were disordered and confusing; he couldn't place the sequence of the fire, the screaming, and the alarms in the right order. At other times, a wave of pure, image-less terror would wash over him while he was reading or drinking tea, his body seized with the full emotional horror of the event without any accompanying picture. The memory, when it did have a shape, felt as if it belonged to someone else, a disturbing film he had been forced to watch.

This profound sense of disconnection from his own experience solidified into a damning self-appraisal: there was something fundamentally wrong with him. The alien quality of the memory was proof to him that his mind, once his most trusted tool, was now defective. This belief that he was broken made the memory fragments feel even more shameful and disjointed, pushing them further away and making them harder to integrate. His body, too, had become an enemy, launching into a state of high alert for no discernible reason. He came to believe he had to be especially careful, that the world was filled with hidden dangers he had previously ignored. This conviction for constant vigilance meant he was perpetually on edge, startled by the clatter of a dropped tray in the hospital cafeteria or the sudden ring of his phone.

The world, which he had navigated with such confidence, was now a minefield of sensory triggers. The smell of his wife's toast burning one morning sent a jolt of panic through him, his heart hammering as if the fire were happening all over again. He felt an immediate, overwhelming sense of threat and had to leave the kitchen, retreating to his study to try and force the rising panic down. This experience, and others like it-the specific warmth of the shower on his skin reminding him of the heat flash-led him to meticulously avoid situations that might provoke a similar reaction. He stopped watching the news, and when his wife put on a medical drama, he would abruptly leave the room. His belief that he was permanently damaged also made him withdraw from sources of comfort; he would push away his wife's affectionate gestures, feeling that positive emotions were a dangerous indulgence when he needed to be on guard.

These interlocking cycles began to tighten around him. His constant state of hypervigilance, driven by his negative beliefs, made his mind scan for danger, which paradoxically made him more likely to recall fragments of the trauma. A sudden sound would not only make him jump, but would also pull the disembodied feeling of heat or the acrid smell into his consciousness. These intrusive fragments of memory would, in turn, spike his sense of immediate threat, convincing him his body was right to be in a constant state of alarm. His attempts to suppress these thoughts were failing; in fact, the effort seemed to make the memory fragments more potent and intrusive when they inevitably broke through. His avoidance also backfired, sensitizing him further, so that even the ambient stress of a busy hospital corridor now felt latently dangerous. In a bizarre departure from his lifelong caution, he started driving too fast, a reckless behavior that felt utterly unlike him but provided a fleeting sense of control.

The breaking point came last week. While observing a procedure, a nurse dropped a metal bowl, and An flinched so violently he knocked over a tray of sterile instruments. There was no danger, but his body had reacted with absolute certainty that there was. The incident crystallized his deepest fear: he was no longer the man he had been. The shame of that moment, combined with his wife's growing distress at his emotional distance, finally prompted him to seek help. He confessed in his first session that he wasn't sure if his mind could be repaired, but he had to try. He wanted his hands, and his life, to feel like his own again.
